issues.legal_issue: A witness’s prior written testimony may be used where the witness admits it was accurately recorded but disowns its truth on a general explanation of pressure, without being confronted separately with every discrepancy.
material_facts: At trial, two witnesses repudiated their earlier testimony given before the committal court.
The prosecutor read the earlier testimony to each witness; each admitted it was accurately recorded but said it was false because of police pressure.
The objection was that each passage differing from the trial testimony had to be put separately to the witness for explanation.
issues.conclusion: The requirements of section 145 of the Indian Evidence Act were satisfied, and the prior testimony could be read as evidence at the trial.
issues.legal_principle: Section 145 of the Indian Evidence Act requires a witness to be confronted with a prior written statement when it is used to contradict the witness. Ordinarily, attention must be drawn to the particular contradictory passages. But where the witness accepts that the prior statement was accurately recorded and gives the same general explanation—that it was false and made under pressure—confronting the witness separately with each discrepancy is unnecessary because the explanation would be the same. The prior committal-court testimony was brought on record under section 288 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.criminal_trial_with_prior_written_testim: A criminal trial used a witness’s earlier written testimony to contradict the witness’s testimony at trial.
predicates.witness_admits_accurate_record: The witness acknowledged that the earlier testimony was accurately recorded.
predicates.witness_disowns_statement_under_general_: The witness denied the truth of the earlier testimony and attributed it generally to pressure.

issues.definition: When a criminal trial uses earlier written testimony and the witness accepts that it was accurately recorded but disowns it on a general claim of pressure, the earlier testimony is admissible for consideration.

issues.legal_issue: A prior statement made under formal examination may corroborate earlier testimony but is not itself evidence.
material_facts: The two witnesses had also made statements under formal examination before a magistrate.
The witnesses’ attention was drawn to passages from those statements, and they explained that the statements had been made under police pressure.
issues.conclusion: The statements made under formal examination were not evidence, but were corroborative of the witnesses’ earlier testimony before the committal court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated statements made under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as not being evidence, while permitting them to corroborate what the witnesses had earlier stated before the committal court. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.criminal_trial_with_prior_testimony: A criminal trial considered testimony previously given by a witness before a committal court.
predicates.witness_made_formal_statement: The witness also made a statement during a formal examination before a magistrate.
predicates.attention_drawn_to_formal_statement: The witness’s attention was drawn at trial to passages from the formal statement.

issues.definition: When a criminal trial considers prior testimony and the witness’s attention is drawn to a separate formal statement, that formal statement serves only to corroborate the prior testimony.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s account of events should not be rejected merely because other witnesses did not hear the same sound, where the account is plausible and corroborated.
material_facts: A witness said he heard a pistol shot and cries from a nearby house, saw the accused leaving together, and later saw a body at the house.
The High Court disbelieved him in part because other witnesses had not heard the pistol shot and because he said he had followed the accused for a short distance at night.
The witness’s account of the shot was corroborated by other evidence, including eyewitness testimony and the discovery of a cartridge at the scene.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to reject the witness’s evidence; the Court accepted it as credible and corroborated.
issues.legal_principle: The Court reasoned that people who are awake may hear a nighttime firearm report that sleeping people do not hear, and that an omission from a report made by someone relying on second-hand information does not necessarily discredit the evidence of those with direct knowledge. The witness’s account was assessed in light of its plausibility and corroboration. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_acquittal: A criminal appeal challenges an acquittal and requires review of evidence rejected by the lower appellate court.
predicates.witness_gives_plausible_direct_observati: A witness described personally hearing or seeing events connected with the alleged offence.
predicates.witness_account_has_independent_corrobor: Other evidence independently supported a material part of the witness’s account.
predicates.other_witnesses_missed_one_detail: One or more other witnesses did not report the same detail, such as hearing a sound.

issues.definition: In an appeal from an acquittal, a plausible account based on direct observation is accepted as corroborated when independent evidence supports it, even if other witnesses missed one detail.

issues.legal_issue: A person who accompanies an armed offender, fires a weapon to facilitate the offender’s attack, and leaves with the offender may be convicted of murder with the offender on the basis of shared participation.
material_facts: The accused father and his son arrived together at the victims’ home, armed respectively with a pistol and a sword, and left together after the attack.
The son attacked the victims and wounded a person who had grappled with him; the father fired his pistol, causing that person to release the son.
A cartridge was found at the scene, and a pistol and cartridges of the same bore were later recovered following information given by the father.
Eyewitness testimony and evidence that the father and son left together supported the prosecution case.
issues.conclusion: The evidence established the father’s participation with the son in the murders; the acquittal was set aside and the father was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. It relied on the combined evidence of the accused arriving and leaving together, being armed, the father firing to enable the son to escape a grapple, and the physical evidence corroborating the eyewitness accounts. No earlier cases are cited.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_acquittal and accused_arrived_with_armed_offender and accused_used_weapon_to_facilitate_attack and accused_left_with_offender and evidence_corroborates_shared_participation

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_acquittal: A criminal appeal challenges an acquittal for an offence committed with another person.
predicates.accused_arrived_with_armed_offender: The accused arrived at the scene with another person who was armed and committed the attack.
predicates.accused_used_weapon_to_facilitate_attack: The accused used a weapon in a way that enabled or assisted the other person’s attack.
predicates.accused_left_with_offender: The accused left the scene together with the person who committed the attack.
predicates.evidence_corroborates_shared_participati: Eyewitness or physical evidence independently supports the accused’s participation with the other offender.

issues.definition: When an appeal against acquittal concerns an accused who arrived armed with an offender, used a weapon to facilitate the attack, left with that offender, and is linked by corroborating evidence, the accused is convicted of shared murder.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for murder supported by eyewitness, confession, and physical evidence is not displaced on appeal merely because the lower courts have already made concurrent findings of guilt.
material_facts: The son was identified as the attacker by eyewitness evidence, including his sister’s earlier committal-court testimony and another eyewitness’s testimony.
The son confessed to a relative that he had committed the murders.
Blood-stained clothing and a shoe were connected to the incident, and a blood-stained sword was recovered after information from the son.
The trial court and High Court had both convicted the son.
issues.conclusion: The son’s appeal was dismissed, and his conviction and sentence were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that it ordinarily does not reassess evidence for a third time where the trial court and High Court have reached concurrent findings, but it considered the evidence and found the prosecution case fully proved. It relied on the evidence as a whole, including eyewitness testimony, the extra-judicial confession, and circumstantial and physical evidence. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this evidentiary conclusion.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: A convicted person brings a criminal appeal challenging the conviction or sentence.
predicates.concurrent_findings_of_guilt: The trial court and the appellate court have both found the accused guilty.
predicates.eyewitness_evidence_supported_by_confess: Eyewitness testimony is supported by a confession and physical or circumstantial evidence linking the accused to the offence.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal challenges concurrent findings of guilt and eyewitness evidence is supported by a confession and physical evidence, the conviction and sentence are upheld.

issues.legal_issue: A lesser sentence may be imposed on a participant whose part in a shared murder was secondary.
material_facts: The father was convicted of murder with his son under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
The father participated by accompanying his son and firing a pistol to enable the son to escape a grapple, but the Court regarded his part in the murders as secondary.
The trial court had imposed a death sentence on the father.
issues.conclusion: The Court replaced the death sentence with a sentence of life imprisonment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and concluded that life imprisonment was sufficient because the father’s part in the murders was secondary. No earlier cases or more detailed sentencing test are cited.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_acquittal: A criminal appeal against acquittal results in the accused being convicted for participation in murder with another person.
predicates.accused_convicted_for_shared_murder: The accused is found guilty of murder committed jointly with another person.
predicates.accused_role_in_murders_is_secondary: The accused participated in the murders, but the court assessed that participation as secondary to the other offender’s role.

issues.definition: When an appeal against acquittal results in a conviction for shared murder and the convicted participant’s role is secondary, the sentence is reduced.
